documents.title: CUNY Academic Integrity Policy (2024)
documents.summary: System-wide CUNY academic integrity policy revised in 2024 to add AI. It writes AI into the definitions of cheating and plagiarism, requires citation of AI content, defers permitted use to each syllabus or instructor, and sets reporting, sanction and hearing procedures plus a rationale for teaching responsible AI use.
documents.stance_why: The policy sets no AI rule of its own beyond classing unauthorized AI use as cheating and plagiarism; it states that 'Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor', which hands the decision to instructors.

units.why: The definition of cheating names 'artificial intelligence (AI) systems' among things whose 'unauthorized use or attempted use' during an academic exercise is cheating; it binds students, defines misuse (general phase), forbids unauthorized use (must-not) and files AI misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: unauthorized use or attempted use of material, information, notes, study aids, devices, artificial intelligence (AI)
units.policy: Unauthorized use or attempted use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems during an academic exercise is cheating.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general with a normalized policy; B coded when-misuse with no policy. The source sentence defines cheating ('is the unauthorized use or attempted use of ... artificial intelligence (AI) systems ... during an academic exercise'), a definition of what counts as misuse rather than a response to suspected misuse, so phase is general. Both coders agreed on student, must-not, P36 and restrict. B's fuller anchor was kept and A's policy wording, which stays within the sentence.

units.why: Listing 'Copying ... from a generative AI system' as an example of cheating bars students from copying AI output into work submitted for credit; P19 (AI may not produce submitted work) fits better than P36 because the rule names the prohibited act.
units.anchor: Copying from another person or from a generative AI system
units.policy: Copying from a generative AI system, as from another person, is an example of cheating.

units.why: The sentence 'Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor' leaves the permission decision to each assignment and instructor, so P04. It binds students (actor) as they do their work (during-work) and is a must; it sets no ban of its own, so the stance is restrict only in the sense of conditioning use.
units.anchor: generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments
units.frag_start: Any use of generative AI tools
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work; both gave student, must, P04, restrict. The sentence tells students that any use must conform to the assignment's usage policy, which governs what they do while working, not how expectations are communicated, so during-work. The fuller 15-word anchor states the rule, so policy is null. B also coded a second unit on the same sentence (instructors define usage policies in the syllabus, P09, should); the source does not instruct instructors to do so but only says where policies are defined, and the sentence is already coded here as P04, so that unit was dropped.

units.why: The sentence lists 'Using artificial intelligence tools to generate content for assignments or exams ... without written authorization from the instructor' as an example of cheating, so students must not have AI produce submitted work unless the instructor authorizes it in writing; P19 fits as the rule is about generating the work submitted.
units.anchor: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate content for assignments or exams
units.frag_start: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate
units.frag_end: without written authorization from the instructor
units.policy: Using artificial intelligence tools, including language models or code generators, to generate content for assignments or exams without written authorization from the instructor is cheating.
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P06 (fallback when a syllabus is silent); phase, actor, modality and stance agreed. P06 requires a rule about what applies when a syllabus says nothing about AI; this sentence never mentions the syllabus or silence, it bans AI-generated content without written instructor authorization and calls it cheating. P19 (do not have AI produce the work you submit) is the closer match, so P19; the authorization condition is kept in the policy text.

units.why: Unauthorized use during an examination of 'any electronic devices ... to copy, retrieve, generate or send information' is cheating, which bans AI-capable devices on exams; P22 (no AI on exams, closed-device rules) fits.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices
units.policy: Unauthorized use of notes, prepared answers, or electronic devices such as cell phones, computers, smart watches, or other technologies during an examination to copy, retrieve, generate or send information is cheating.

units.why: The sentence forbids 'Submitting content generated by another person or an AI tool ... as solely your own work'. This is the ownership principle, that submitted work must be one's own, so P29.
units.anchor: Submitting content generated by another person or an AI tool or any other source as
units.policy: Submitting content generated by another person or an AI tool or any other source as solely your own work is cheating.

units.why: The clause lists 'content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation' submitted as one's own as cheating, so AI-altered content is acceptable when properly cited and students must cite it; P24 (disclose AI use), must, with unit_stance permit because citing is the condition for use.
units.anchor: content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation
units.policy: Submitting content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation is cheating.
units.resolution_why: A coded must/permit, B coded must-not/restrict; both P24, student, during-work. The text forbids submitting AI-generated or AI-altered content 'without proper citation', and what students have to do to stay within the rule is cite. The same coders coded the parallel plagiarism clauses (quotation marks and citations, citing the AI as the source) as must/permit, so must/permit keeps the three citation rules consistent. The policy keeps the source's 'is cheating' framing.

units.why: Plagiarism is defined to include copying 'an AI tool's actual words or images without the use of quotation marks and citations'. This requires quotation and citation of AI output, so P24 (cite AI use); the misconduct label is secondary.
units.anchor: Copying another person’s or an AI tool’s actual words or images without the use of
units.policy: Copying an AI tool's actual words or images without quotation marks and citations attributing the words to their source is plagiarism.

units.why: The plagiarism list includes 'Unauthorized use of AI-generated content', which classes unauthorized AI use as plagiarism, a definition of misuse (general) that students must not breach; P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content is plagiarism.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B when-misuse; other codes agreed (student, must-not, P36, restrict). The line is a definition of what plagiarism includes, not a statement about handling suspected misuse, so general.

units.why: The same sentence makes use of AI-generated content 'even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source' plagiarism, a separate rule that paraphrasing does not remove the duty to cite; P24.
units.anchor: even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source
units.policy: Use of AI-generated content, whether in whole or in part, even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source is plagiarism.

units.why: The sentence states that 'Penalties for academic dishonesty include academic sanctions, such as failing or otherwise reduced grades'; it informs students of the penalties that apply to the AI misconduct defined in the policy, so P37, informs, student.
units.anchor: Penalties for academic dishonesty include academic sanctions, such as failing or otherwise reduced grades
units.policy: Penalties for academic dishonesty include academic sanctions, such as failing or otherwise reduced grades, and/or disciplinary sanctions, including suspension or expulsion.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B student; phase when-misuse, informs, P37 and neutral agreed. The sentence tells students what penalties academic dishonesty carries, so actor is student. It does not name AI; it is kept because it states the sanctions for the AI misconduct defined in the same policy.

units.why: The policy says the Academic Integrity Officer 'should seek disciplinary sanctions only if' there is a substantial violation and names 'generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization' as an example, so the passage directs the officer's action on AI misuse; admin, when-misuse, should, P37, restrict.
units.anchor: generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization
units.frag_start: Examples of substantial violations include but
units.policy: Generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization is an example of a substantial violation, for which the Academic Integrity Officer should seek disciplinary sanctions.
units.resolution_why: A coded modality should, B informs; other codes agreed. The controlling sentence tells the Officer what to do ('should seek disciplinary sanctions') and names AI generation of entire assignments as an example of a substantial violation, so should fits better than informs. A's policy wording was kept, since it stays within the sentence.

units.why: A reduced grade 'may be an F' set by the faculty member states a concrete academic penalty available to instructors for violations including AI misuse; P37.
units.anchor: A reduced grade may be an "F" or another grade that is lower
units.frag_start: The reduced grade may apply to the
units.frag_end: would have earned but for the violation
units.policy: A reduced grade may be an F or another grade lower than the grade the student would have earned but for the violation, applied to the assignment or the course grade at the faculty member's discretion.

units.why: The policy requires each college to 'subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service', a similarity-checking tool; AI is not named, but it is the type for plagiarism software used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: Each college shall subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service
units.frag_start: Each college shall subscribe to an
units.frag_end: available for use by the faculty

units.why: 'faculty should inform students of their use' tells instructors to tell students when detection services are used; it is about detection tools (P40), not instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: faculty should inform students of their use
units.policy: Faculty should inform students of the use of electronic plagiarism detection services.

units.why: 'shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible' asks instructors to talk with the student before reporting, which is P57.
units.anchor: shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible

units.why: The faculty member 'shall report such incident on a Faculty Report Form' to the Academic Integrity Officer, routing violations (including AI misuse) into the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: shall report such incident on a Faculty Report Form
units.policy: A faculty member who concludes there has been an incident of academic dishonesty sufficient to affect the student's final course grade reports it on a Faculty Report Form submitted to the college's Academic Integrity Officer, copying the Department Chair.

units.why: The procedure for a student who denies the charge guarantees 'written notice of the charges' and 'the right to appear before the Committee', a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: written notice of the charges against them; (ii) the right to appear before the Committee
units.frag_start: These procedures, at a minimum, shall
units.policy: Procedures for hearing cases in which a student denies academic dishonesty provide students at a minimum with written notice of the charges, the right to appear before the Committee, and the right to present witness statements and/or to call witnesses.

units.why: A student who admits dishonesty but contests the sanction 'may appeal the academic sanction through the college's grade appeal process', another route to respond to the outcome of an allegation (P64).

units.why: The EXPLANATION says the revision is needed because the policy 'does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence' and that preparing students to use AI 'responsibly and ethically is critical'. It is the stated purpose for the AI amendment, so P56 (institution-wide framework preamble).
units.anchor: the current policy does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence and its use by

units.why: The Explanation says 'Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical to the University's mission', an institution-level statement of purpose and principle, so P56, informs, admin; it welcomes responsible AI use, so unit_stance encourage.
units.anchor: Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical to the
units.resolution_why: A coded P44 with actor all; B coded P56 with actor admin; both informs and encourage. The sentence is the University's own statement of mission and principle ('critical to the University's mission, to ensuring academic integrity'), not a statement that courses teach AI use as a professional skill, so P56 (institution-wide framework) fits better than P44; the statement is made by the institution, so admin. The anchor alone states the principle, so policy is null.

units.why: The Explanation says 'students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively in today's world and to prepare for their AI-assisted careers', a rationale about students' need for AI skill, so P44 (effective AI use as a professional skill), informs, student; it welcomes AI use, so encourage.
units.anchor: students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively in today's world
units.frag_end: careers and lives in the future
units.resolution_why: A coded actor student, B admin; both informs, P44, encourage. The sentence concerns what students must become able to do, so student is kept. The wording is a rationale rather than an instruction, hence informs.

units.why: The policy says each college 'may adopt its own more specific procedures to implement the Policy' provided they are consistent; it permits colleges to add procedures and sets an institution-wide framework, so P56, admin, may.
units.anchor: may adopt its own more specific procedures to implement the Policy
units.policy: Each college may adopt its own more specific procedures to implement the Policy, which must be consistent with the Policy.
units.resolution_why: A coded must with a policy merging 'shall implement' and 'may adopt'; B coded may. The anchor sentence has two rules ('shall implement this Policy' and 'may adopt its own more specific procedures'); the unit stays on the second, which is the load-bearing rule for local variation, and keeps the consistency condition from the next sentence. Modality therefore may; P56, admin, before-course agreed.

documents.title: AI and Academic Integrity (LibGuide)
documents.summary: A Hunter Libraries guide page on AI and academic integrity. It warns about unreliable AI citations, recommends transparency, quotes the AI parts of the CUNY policy, and reproduces Chicago Manual of Style guidance on citing chatbot content.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no rule of its own; it recommends transparency, quotes the CUNY policy that AI use must follow 'the usage policy for specific assignments', and gives citation guidance, so the decision on use stays with instructors and assignments.

units.why: The guide warns of 'inconsistency across all varieties of AI tools in providing context and citation', which tells students AI output cannot be trusted to be sourced; P31 (verify AI output).
units.anchor: inconsistency across all varieties of AI tools in providing context and citation
units.frag_start: One of the biggest challenges with using
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence. The guide says 'inconsistency across all varieties of AI tools in providing context and citation for the information it generates' is a main challenge, a real statement of AI risk for citation and sourcing, so it is kept as P31 informs; B coded only the following sentence.

units.why: 'we also cannot be confident in declaring that no AI tool does' hallucinate sources: AI tools may give false information or fake citations, a warning to verify output, P31.
units.anchor: Not all AI tools hallucinate sources or generate false information

units.why: The guide names 'Citing AI tools and AI generated information (including hallucinated citations or false information)' among its biggest academic-integrity concerns, which warns that AI output and citations can be false; P31 (AI output can be wrong), informs, student.
units.anchor: Citing AI tools and AI generated information (including hallucinated citations or false information)
units.resolution_why: A coded P24, B coded P31; informs, student, neutral agreed. The line is part of a list of concerns and its parenthesis, 'hallucinated citations or false information', is about unreliable AI output; it does not tell students to disclose anything, so P31 fits better than P24 (the disclosure rules are coded in the units that state them).

units.why: The guide advises to 'be as transparent as possible when using an AI tool for your research', a recommendation to disclose AI use; P24.

The same coders coded the parallel plagiarism clauses (quotation marks and citations, citing the AI as the source) as must/permit, so must/permit keeps the three citation rules consistent. The policy keeps the source's 'is cheating' framing.
